scenes.title: hook (what did each run out of?)

voiceover.text: Here's the loop from last time, inside a ring of seven systems. Now compare two athletes. A powerlifter can lift more than almost anyone, and is spent after six seconds. A marathon runner keeps going for two hours, but can't lift anything like as much. So what did each one run out of? And if they swapped events, which system would fail first?

Start with one movement: a netball shot. All seven systems are involved, but on very different clocks. The digestive system supplied the glucose hours ago, and right now it's turned down, so blood can go elsewhere. Adrenaline was released minutes before, raising heart rate and releasing fuel. Breathing and heart rate had already risen before the ball arrived. Then, in milliseconds, the nervous system spots the ball and fires the commands, the muscles pull, and the skeleton's levers turn that pull into the shot. So the body anticipates. It doesn't just react. And a system can help by being turned down.

Every movement uses all seven systems, so that can't tell a lift from a marathon. The useful question is which system reaches its limit first. That's the limiting system. In a maximal lift, it's nervous and muscular: how many big motor units you can fire at once. In a hundred-metre sprint, it's the muscles' fast fuel, which runs low within about ten seconds. In a four-hundred, by-products build up faster than the blood can clear them. On a three-hour hike, it's glycogen, fluid and salt. To justify it, look at how the performer fails. Slowing while still moving well means fuel. A gymnast whose landings wobble late in a routine, while she still has power, points to the nervous system. So the lifter and the runner trained different limiting systems.

To analyse a movement, split it into phases. Take a vertical jump. In preparation, the hips, knees and ankles bend, and the quadriceps lengthen under tension: an eccentric contraction that loads them like a spring. In execution, the same muscles shorten hard, concentrically, recruiting the big fast units, and the levers drive you up. In follow-through, stabilisers control the body in the air, and proprioception gets ready to land. In recovery, the landing is absorbed eccentrically again. Name the contraction in every phase, and don't stop at execution. The landing is where the injury risk is.

When movement goes wrong, first aid steps in. It's the immediate care given before professional help arrives, and it has four jobs, in order. Preserve life. Stop it getting worse. Help recovery start. And decide what happens next: play on, stop, see a doctor, or call an ambulance. That last job is the one most often done badly. But first aid has limits. It can't rule out a fracture, it can't clear a concussion, and it can't fix why the injury happened.

scenes.title: two plans, and every step is a gate

voiceover.text: Two plans organise it. For someone who isn't responding, use DRSABCD: check for Danger, check for a Response, Send for help, open the Airway, check Breathing, start CPR if they aren't breathing normally, and attach a Defibrillator. Danger comes first, because a second casualty helps nobody. For a conscious, injured athlete, use TOTAPS: Talk, Observe, Touch, then Active movement, Passive movement, and finally a Skills test. Each step is a gate. If they can't move the joint themselves, you stop there, and they don't play.

The syllabus names three situations. First, inefficient movement: poor technique, fatigue or a skipped warm-up. That usually means a soft tissue injury. A sprain is a ligament, a strain is a muscle or tendon, and a contusion is a bruise. Manage it with RICER: rest, ice, compression, elevation and referral, with ice for about twenty minutes every two hours. And avoid HARM: heat, alcohol, running and massage, which all increase blood flow and swelling. Deformity, a sound at the moment of injury, or not being able to bear weight means a doctor decides.

Second, dehydration. As you saw with the delivery chain, sweat lowers plasma volume, so heart rate rises and the body sheds heat less well. The signs come in order: thirst and dark urine, then headache and a racing heart, then cramps and dizziness, then confusion. For mild cases, stop, find shade and sip cool fluid, and don't return to play. Heat exhaustion means lie them down, cool them and get medical help. But treat confusion in a hot athlete as heat stroke. That's an emergency. Call an ambulance, cool them hard, and follow DRSABCD.

scenes.title: undue stress, and where first aid stops

voiceover.text: Third, undue stress on the body: more load than the body is ready for. Here the harm builds up. Overuse injuries, like stress fractures and shin pain, mean stop and refer. Never put a collapse after hard effort down to tiredness: follow DRSABCD and get help. Chest pain or collapse during exercise means an ambulance, and CPR with a defibrillator if they're not breathing normally. So first aid is essential, but it treats the event, not the cause.
Two things to remember. How a performer fails names the system that failed. And first aid is essential, but not enough on its own.

Two exam questions. First. A footballer is still running well in the last ten minutes, but their passes keep going astray. Identify the likely limiting system, and justify your choice. Pause here to answer.

It's the nervous system. The legs are still working, so fuel and oxygen aren't the limit. What's failing is accuracy, and late in a game, fatigue cuts the brain's drive and slows decisions, so technique breaks down first. The classic mistake is blaming the heart and lungs.
Second. Discuss the role first aid plays in response to movement. Pause here to answer.

Discuss needs both sides. Give the four jobs: preserve life, prevent worsening, promote recovery, and decide what happens next. Use the three situations as evidence. Then the limits: it can't exclude a fracture, clear a concussion or fix the cause. End with a judgement: essential, but not enough. The classic mistake is just listing the acronyms.

So, to analyse any movement, ask which system runs out first, and how you can tell. Now take the shortest race there is. Over the last twenty metres of a hundred, even the fastest sprinters slow down. Why?
